Any authenticated shopper who writes show_tool_calls=true in their own cookie jar sees the view that frontend/src/app/administration/administration.component.html:96 presents as an administrator-only toggle.

Impact: Disclosure of the chatbot's internal tool names and raw invocation arguments to any authenticated user, revealing the backend functions the assistant can drive and the parameters it passes, which maps the attack surface for prompt-injection attempts.

Risk: Medium (likelihood High, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-200
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
chat-conversation.component.ts:68 sets showToolCalls from the cookie value alone with no role comparison, while line 161 appends deltaToolCalls to the message irrespective of the flag — proving the concealment is presentational only and the data has already crossed to the client.
- frontend/src/app/chatbot/chat-conversation/chat-conversation.component.ts:68

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-058 (F-058)
threats.mitigation:
M-056 — Stop exposing internal information to clients (priority P3, effort Medium)
1. Stop emitting deltaToolCalls in the chat stream for callers whose server-verified role is not admin, so the payload never reaches a non-admin browser.
2. Replace the cookie read at frontend/src/app/chatbot/chat-conversation/chat-conversation.component.ts:68 with a role check derived from the verified session, keeping the cookie as a display preference only.
3. Add a test that requests the chat stream as a non-admin user with show_tool_calls=true set and asserts no tool-call chunk appears in the response.
Verification: Set show_tool_calls=true as a standard user, send a message that triggers a tool call, and assert the streamed response contains no tool_calls payload and the UI shows none.
Reference: https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm072025-system-prompt-leakage/

threats.title: [F-059] Test credential pair in shipped bundle (login.component.ts:62)
threats.description:
LoginComponent declares testingUsername and testingPassword as public string literals at frontend/src/app/login/login.component.ts:61 and :62, so the credential pair testing@juice-sh.op / IamU**** (17 chars) is compiled into the production JavaScript bundle that every anonymous visitor downloads. Whether that account exists on the server is not observable from this component, but the literal is a reusable credential shipped to untrusted clients and available to anyone who reads the bundle.

Impact: Anyone who downloads the application bundle learns a valid-looking account name and password for the deployment, giving an unauthenticated attacker a credential to try before any brute-force effort is needed.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-798
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: stride

Evidence:
login.component.ts:61 and :62 assign a fixed email and password as public class fields of a component that is part of the main application bundle, with no environment gating or build-time replacement around them.
- frontend/src/app/login/login.component.ts:62

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-059 (F-059)
threats.mitigation:
M-057 — Move secrets to a managed secret store (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Delete the testingUsername and testingPassword fields at frontend/src/app/login/login.component.ts:61 and :62 and inject any required test identity from the e2e harness instead.
2. Ensure the corresponding server-side account is either removed or provisioned with a random secret in every non-development deployment.
3. Add a build check that fails when a password-like literal appears in the emitted frontend bundle.
Verification: Build the frontend and grep the emitted bundle for IamU**** (17 chars); the build check must report zero matches.
Reference: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/798.html

data.name: SQLite3 Database
data.description: SQLite3 storage backend managed by Sequelize ORM running in the application tier. Persists users, payment cards, addresses, orders, products, feedback, challenge completion state, and security question answers. Seeded at startup from the static YAML definitions in data/static/.

threats.title: [F-008] Hard-coded account credentials in seed data (data/static/users.yml:3)
threats.description:
An attacker reads `data/static/users.yml` in the public repository and finds six seeded administrator passwords in plaintext: admin/admi**** (8 chars) at line 3, support at line 115, J12934 at line 141, wurstbrot at line 150, testing at line 272, and demo at line 215. Because every deployment seeds from the same file, the attacker authenticates against any instance as administrator using any of these credentials.

Impact: An attacker achieves complete administrator takeover of the persisted application state. The database holds user credentials, payment cards, addresses, orders, and challenge completion records for every user.

Risk: Critical (likelihood High, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-798
CVSS v4: 9.3 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:L/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N)
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
data/static/users.yml:3 stores the literal password 'admi**** (8 chars)' for the account at line 2 whose role at line 5 is 'admin'; six further seeded accounts carry literal passwords with the same admin role.
- data/static/users.yml:3

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-008 (F-008)
threats.mitigation:
M-008 — Move secrets to a managed secret store (priority P1, effort Medium)
1. Delete the `password:` literals for every entry in `data/static/users.yml` whose `role` is not 'customer', and resolve those credentials at startup from environment variables or a secret store so each deployment seeds a distinct value.
2. Make the seeding path fail fast when a privileged account's credential variable is unset instead of falling back to a built-in default.
3. Rotate the admin, support, `J12934`, `wurstbrot`, testing and demo credentials on every already-deployed instance and invalidate existing sessions.
Verification: Run `grep -n "password:" data/static/users.yml` — no entry carrying `role: 'admin'` may return a literal; then start the application with the credential environment variables unset and confirm startup aborts instead of creating a default administrator.
Reference: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/798.html

threats.title: [F-019] Hard-coded TOTP secret for admin account (data/static/users.yml:151)
threats.description:
An attacker copies the fixed base32 TOTP seed `IFTXE3SPOEYVURT2MRYGI52TKJ4HC3KH` from `data/static/users.yml:151` and generates valid six-digit codes offline for the administrator account `wurstbrot`. Because the same shared secret is seeded into each database rather than enrolled per instance, the attacker passes the second authentication factor on every deployment.

Impact: The second authentication factor protecting an administrator account provides no additional assurance, so any password compromise escalates directly to full administrative access to stored credentials, payment data and personal data.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact High)
CWE: CWE-321
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
`data/static/users.yml:151` seeds a literal `totpSecret` for the account declared at line 148 with `role: 'admin'` at line 153, so the MFA shared secret is identical in every database created from this seed.
- data/static/users.yml:151

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-019 (F-019)
threats.mitigation:
M-018 — Move cryptographic keys to a managed secret store (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Remove the `totpSecret` literal from `data/static/users.yml` and have the seeding path either generate a cryptographically random secret per deployment or leave MFA unenrolled until the account owner completes enrollment.
2. Re-enroll MFA for the affected account on deployed instances and reject the published secret value at enrollment time.
3. Add a regression test asserting that two consecutive seed runs produce different TOTP secrets for the same account.
Verification: Run `grep -n "totpSecret" data/static/users.yml` and expect zero matches; seed two fresh databases and confirm the stored TOTP secrets differ.
Reference: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/321.html

threats.title: [F-034] Cleartext payment card data at rest (data/static/users.yml:22)
threats.description:
An attacker who obtains read access to the SQLite file — through a co-located process in the same container, a backup copy, or any file-read primitive in the application — extracts full payment card numbers with cardholder name and expiry directly, because the card records are persisted as cleartext columns and the database file carries no encryption.

Impact: Full payment card records plus the linked names, postal addresses and mobile numbers in the same seed become readable from a single file copy, exposing every stored customer's payment and personal data at once.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-311
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
data/static/users.yml:22 persists a full 16-digit card number together with cardholder name and expiry at lines 21-24, and the component's control inventory records no database-level encryption for the SQLite file.
- data/static/users.yml:22

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-034 (F-034)
threats.mitigation:
M-032 — Stop persisting full card numbers in cleartext in the card table (priority P2, effort High)
1. Replace the stored full card number with a token plus the last four digits and expiry, so no persisted column holds a complete PAN; where the full value is genuinely required, encrypt it with an application-held key that is not stored in the database file.
2. Enable encryption for the SQLite file itself (for example SQLCipher) and restrict the file to the application's own OS user.
3. Add a test that seeds a database and asserts that no column value matches a full card-number pattern.
Verification: Seed a fresh database and run the new test plus `strings` over the database file: neither may reveal a complete 16-digit card number in cleartext.
Reference: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cryptographic_Storage_Cheat_Sheet.html

threats.title: [F-041] Cleartext recovery answers for admin accounts (data/static/users.yml:8)
threats.description:
An attacker reads the cleartext security-question answer seeded for the administrator account at data/static/users.yml:8, matches it to the question text in data/static/securityQuestions.yml, and drives the account-recovery path to set a new password for that administrator without ever knowing the original one.

Impact: The account-recovery factor guarding administrator accounts is public knowledge, allowing an unauthenticated attacker to seize administrator identity and with it every stored credential, payment card and personal record.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact High)
CWE: CWE-522
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
data/static/users.yml:8 stores the recovery answer for the account at line 2 whose role at line 5 is 'admin' as a cleartext literal; further answers at lines 112, 120, 146 and 156 belong to accounts likewise seeded with `role: 'admin'`, and several answers at lines 37, 68 and 175 are annotated with the public source that reveals them.
- data/static/users.yml:8

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-041 (F-041)
threats.mitigation:
M-039 — Hash security answers and remove the literals from the seed file (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Persist security answers only as salted hashes using the same key-derivation function as passwords, and compare candidate answers against the hash instead of the stored string.
2. Delete the cleartext answers for privileged accounts from data/static/users.yml and stop seeding a recovery factor for any account with an administrative role.
3. Add a test asserting that the persisted security-answer column never equals the literal from the seed file.
Verification: Seed a fresh database and query the security-answer column for the admin account: the stored value must not equal '@xI98PxDO+06!' and must have the length and format of the configured hash.
Reference: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Choosing_and_Using_Security_Questions_Cheat_Sheet.html

data.name: Socket.IO Real-Time Layer
data.description: Socket.IO v3 real-time event hub running on the same Express/Node.js server process as the API (port 3000). Handles scoreboard push updates, challenge-solved notifications, and hacking-instructor progress events. Registered via lib/startup/registerWebsocketEvents.ts at server startup.

threats.title: [F-021] Unauthenticated WebSocket Channel
threats.description:
An anonymous internet client completes the Socket.IO handshake on port 3000 and is accepted by the connection handler registered at line 23. The handler installs no io.use() middleware, never reads socket.handshake.auth, and never applies the JWT check that guards the REST API, so the socket is trusted without any identity. From that socket the attacker receives every buffered challenge-solved notification and emits the state-changing notification received and verify* events.

Impact: Any unauthenticated internet client joins the real-time channel, reads the full notification stream, and reaches the four server-side event handlers that mutate challenge and notification state for every user of the deployment.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-306
CVSS v4: 6.9 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:L/VI:L/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N)
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
Line 23 is the only connection handler in the component and it performs no identity check; a grep for io.use, allowRequest, handshake.auth, verifyClient, isAuthorized and authenticat across the component path returns zero hits.
- lib/startup/registerWebsocketEvents.ts:23

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-1 external → api-server (internet-facing): The Socket.IO handshake reaches the same Express server that tb-1 guards, but the connection handler applies no equivalent of security.isAuthorized().

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-021 (F-021)
threats.mitigation:
M-020 — Require authentication on every exposed endpoint (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Register an io.use((socket, next) => ...) middleware before io.on('connection') that reads the token from socket.handshake.auth, verifies it with the same helper lib/insecurity.ts uses for security.isAuthorized(), attaches the resolved principal to the socket, and calls next(new Error('unauthorized')) when verification fails.
2. Add an integration test that connects a socket-io client without a token and asserts a connect_error, and a second test that connects with a valid token and asserts the connection succeeds.
Verification: Run node -e "const io=require('socket.io-client');const s=io('http://localhost:3000',{transports:['websocket']});s.on('connect',()=>console.log('CONNECTED'));s.on('connect_error',e=>console.log('REJECTED',e.message));" and expect REJECTED instead of CONNECTED.
Reference: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/306.html

threats.title: [F-042] Client-side security enforcement (lib/startup/registerWebsocketEvents.ts:50)
threats.description:
The verifyCloseNotificationsChallenge handler marks the challenge solved when the client-supplied payload is an array longer than one element, which is the client's own assertion that it performed the action. The same pattern appears at lines 41 and 45, where the client supplies the string that is matched against the expected payload. Any socket therefore promotes global challenge state without performing the gameplay the challenge represents.

Impact: Any client, authenticated or not, forges completion of the three socket-verified challenges, corrupting the scoreboard and progress state that the deployment treats as the record of who achieved what.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-602
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
Line 50 passes a predicate over the client-controlled data argument straight into challengeUtils.solveIf, so the client's claim is the only proof of completion; the handler consults no server-side record of what the client actually did.
- lib/startup/registerWebsocketEvents.ts:50

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-1 external → api-server (internet-facing): The handler grants challenge progress behind tb-1 on the client's own assertion, without the identity-based resource check the boundary's authorization leg assumes.

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-042 (F-042)
threats.mitigation:
M-040 — Enforce authorization on the server (priority P2, effort High)
1. Resolve the socket's authenticated principal and gate each verify* handler on server-side evidence that the action occurred, such as a recorded request or a stored artifact, instead of on the client-supplied data argument.
2. Add a test that emits each verify* event with a forged payload from a socket that performed no gameplay and asserts the corresponding challenge stays unsolved.
Verification: Emit verifyCloseNotificationsChallenge with [1,2] from a socket-io client on a fresh instance and assert through the project's challenge API test helper that closeNotificationsChallenge.solved is still false.
Reference: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/602.html

threats.title: [F-060] Sensitive data exposure (lib/startup/registerWebsocketEvents.ts:30)
threats.description:
On every connection the handler iterates the process-global notifications cache and emits each entry to the new socket at line 30, with no filter for the recipient. Each notification object carries a flag property, as the findIndex destructuring at line 34 shows, so a client receives the flag values of challenges solved by other users of the same deployment.

Impact: Challenge flag codes earned by other users are disclosed to every client that connects, which in a scored deployment lets a participant submit flags for challenges they never solved.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-200
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
Line 30 emits every entry of the shared notifications cache to each connecting socket, and line 34 shows those entries carry a flag field; no recipient scoping exists between the cache and the emit.
- lib/startup/registerWebsocketEvents.ts:30

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-060 (F-060)
threats.mitigation:
M-058 — Stop exposing internal information to clients (priority P3, effort Medium)
1. Store the owning principal with each notification and replay only that principal's notifications to a connecting socket, and omit the flag field from notifications emitted to any other recipient.
2. Add a test in which user A solves a challenge and user B connects, asserting B receives no notification carrying A's flag.
Verification: Solve one challenge as user A, connect a second client as user B, and assert the notifications B receives contain no flag value belonging to A.
Reference: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/200.html

threats.title: [F-064] Unbounded connection resource use (lib/startup/registerWebsocketEvents.ts:29)
threats.description:
Each accepted connection runs the notifications.forEach replay at line 29 and registers four event handlers, and nothing caps how many connections one client opens or how fast it opens them. An attacker loops unauthenticated handshakes against port 3000, and because the Socket.IO server shares the Node process and event loop with the REST API, the serialization and emit work plus the retained socket state degrade the whole application.

Impact: Connection flooding consumes event-loop time and memory in the same process that serves the REST API, degrading or stalling the application for all users.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-400
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
Line 29 performs per-connection work proportional to the notifications cache for every socket; a grep for rateLimit, maxHttpBufferSize, connectTimeout and throttle across the component path returns zero hits, and the Server options at line 20 set only cors.
- lib/startup/registerWebsocketEvents.ts:29

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-064 (F-064)
threats.mitigation:
M-062 — Rate-limit expensive requests and bound input size (priority P3, effort Medium)
1. Pass maxHttpBufferSize and connectTimeout to the Server constructor and reject handshakes above a per-IP connection and rate threshold in an io.use() middleware or the reverse proxy in front of port 3000.
2. Add a load test that opens connections past the configured threshold and asserts further handshakes are refused while existing REST requests still return within the normal latency budget.
Verification: Open connections past the configured per-IP limit with a socket-io client loop and assert the excess handshakes fail while GET /rest/admin/application-version still responds under one second.
Reference: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/400.html

data.name: CI/CD Pipeline
data.description: Continuous-integration / deployment workflows (.github/workflows/ci.yml, .github/workflows/codeql-analysis.yml, .github/workflows/frontend-bundle-analysis.yml, .github/workflows/image_actions.yml, …). Build and release automation holding repository, registry and deploy credentials, with supply-chain reach into the produced artifact.

threats.title: [F-018] Unattested container image publish (.github/workflows/ci.yml:327)
threats.description:
An attacker who obtains the long-lived DOCKERHUB_TOKEN held in repository secrets authenticates to Docker Hub as the project and pushes a backdoored bkimminich/juice-shop:latest. The workflow publishes with push: true and emits no provenance attestation or signature, so a pulled image carries nothing a consumer can check against the real build. Every downstream docker pull and docker-compose deployment accepts the impersonated artifact as the project's own.

Impact: A stolen registry token yields publisher impersonation: a malicious image served under the project's own name to every downstream puller, with no attestation for a consumer or an incident responder to distinguish it from a genuine build.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-345
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: stride

Evidence:
.github/workflows/ci.yml:327 authenticates the docker job with the static secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN credential and line 343 sets push: true; a zero-hit search of the same file for provenance, attest, id-token and sbom: confirms no attestation, OIDC trusted publishing, or signing step exists in the publish path.
- .github/workflows/ci.yml:327

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-018 (F-018)
threats.mitigation:
M-017 — Verify token signatures before trusting claims (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Add permissions: id-token: write, attestations: write and contents: read to the docker job in .github/workflows/ci.yml, then set provenance: mode=max and sbom: true on the docker/build-push-action step at line 338 so each push carries an in-toto attestation.
2. Add an actions/attest-build-provenance step after the push and enable Docker Hub OIDC / a short-lived registry token so secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN can be revoked.
3. Add a CI assertion that runs cosign verify-attestation (or docker buildx imagetools inspect) against the freshly pushed tag and fails the job when no provenance predicate is present.
Verification: Run `docker buildx imagetools inspect bkimminich/juice-shop:latest --format '{{ json .Provenance }}'` after a develop build; expect a non-empty in-toto SLSA provenance predicate naming the workflow and commit SHA instead of the current null.
Reference: https://slsa.dev/spec/v1.0/provenance

threats.title: [F-029] Dependency lockfile disabled by configuration (.npmrc:1)
threats.description:
The repository sets package-lock=false, so no lockfile is ever generated and every npm install in CI and in the container build resolves the full transitive dependency graph fresh against the live npm registry. An attacker who gains a momentary version window on any transitive dependency through typosquatting, maintainer account takeover, or a poisoned new release gets that version installed into the next build with no diff, no lockfile baseline, and no integrity hash to reject it.

Impact: A single poisoned transitive package version is installed unnoticed into the published bkimminich/juice-shop image and into the packaged release tarball, executing attacker code both at build time through install hooks and at runtime in every deployment.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-829
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: stride

Evidence:
.npmrc:1 contains package-lock=false, which suppresses lockfile generation outright; .gitignore:10 additionally ignores package-lock.json, and no package-lock.json exists in the working tree. A zero-hit search for `npm ci` across .github/workflows/ and Dockerfile confirms no build path uses a locked install: Dockerfile:5 runs `npm install --omit=dev` and ci.yml lines 51, 71, 110, 147, 203, 238 and 292 all run plain `npm install`, which additionally executes dependency lifecycle scripts (only the lint job at ci.yml:36-38 passes --ignore-scripts).
- .npmrc:1

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-029 (F-029)
threats.mitigation:
M-027 — Pin third-party dependencies to immutable versions (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Delete the package-lock=false line from .npmrc and the package-lock.json entry at .gitignore:10, run npm install once to generate the lockfile, and commit it for both the root and frontend workspaces.
2. Replace every `npm install` in .github/workflows/ci.yml and `npm install --omit=dev` at Dockerfile:5 with `npm ci --ignore-scripts` (adding --omit=dev where production-only install is intended), so builds install exactly the locked, integrity-hashed versions.
3. Add actions/dependency-review-action to the pull_request path so a PR that changes the lockfile is checked for known-vulnerable or malicious packages before merge.
Verification: Run `npm ci --dry-run` in a clean clone; expect it to succeed against a committed package-lock.json instead of the current `npm ci can only install with an existing package-lock.json` error.
Reference: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/829.html

threats.title: [F-030] Mutable Action reference (.github/workflows/image_actions.yml:33)
threats.description:
An attacker who compromises the calibreapp/image-actions repository or its maintainer account pushes malicious code to the main branch. The next image-touching commit on master or develop resolves calibreapp/image-actions@main to that code and executes it on the runner with secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN passed in at line 35, letting the attacker read repository secrets available to the job and commit to the repository through the peter-evans/create-pull-request@v8 step.

Impact: Arbitrary attacker code executes inside the build pipeline holding GITHUB_TOKEN and, in ci.yml, adjacent registry and deployment secrets, giving the supply-chain attacker a path to commit backdoors to the repository and to the published container image.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-1357
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: stride

Evidence:
.github/workflows/image_actions.yml:33 pins a third-party action to the mutable branch ref @main while line 35 hands it secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN; lines 30 and 42 use the equally mutable actions/checkout@v6 and peter-evans/create-pull-request@v8. The same anti-pattern appears at .github/workflows/ci.yml:188 (coverallsapp/github-action@v2, given secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN at line 190) and .github/workflows/codeql-analysis.yml:23, 34 and 36 (github/codeql-action@v3 in a job holding security-events: write), against a repository that otherwise SHA-pins every action.
- .github/workflows/image_actions.yml:33

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-3 external → ci-cd-pipeline (internet-facing): tb-3 assumes CI executes verified code, but a branch-ref action resolves to whatever the third-party repository holds at run time, so the code crossing the boundary is unvalidated.

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-030 (F-030)
threats.mitigation:
M-028 — Set least-privilege CI workflow permissions (priority P2, effort Low)
1. Replace calibreapp/image-actions@main, actions/checkout@v6 and peter-evans/create-pull-request@v8 in .github/workflows/image_actions.yml, coverallsapp/github-action@v2 in .github/workflows/ci.yml:188, and the three github/codeql-action@v3 refs in .github/workflows/codeql-analysis.yml with full 40-character commit SHAs plus a trailing version comment, matching the existing style at ci.yml:29.
2. Enable Dependabot for the github-actions ecosystem so SHA pins are proposed for update rather than left stale.
3. Add a CI step running zizmor or actionlint in the workflow-lint job that fails when any `uses:` value does not match a 40-hex SHA.
Verification: Run `grep -rEn 'uses: [^ ]+@(?![0-9a-f]{40})' .github/workflows/`; expect zero matches once every third-party action is SHA-pinned.
Reference: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/security-for-github-actions/security-guides/security-hardening-for-github-actions#using-third-party-actions

threats.title: [F-040] Missing workflow permissions block (.github/workflows/ci.yml:190)
threats.description:
Neither the CI/CD Pipeline workflow nor the image-compression workflow declares a permissions: key, so every job runs with the repository default GITHUB_TOKEN scope instead of read-only contents. That token is handed to third-party actions, including the mutable coverallsapp/github-action@v2 reference. A compromised step therefore inherits whatever the repository default grants, and the create-pull-request step in image_actions.yml proves the inherited scope already includes repository write, so the step can commit code, publish packages, or create releases.

Impact: Any compromised action or dependency in these workflows escalates from build execution to repository write, allowing an attacker to commit a backdoor to develop or master, publish packages, or create releases under the project's identity.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-732
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: stride

Evidence:
A zero-hit search for `permissions:` across .github/workflows/ci.yml and .github/workflows/image_actions.yml confirms no scope declaration in either file, while only codeql-analysis.yml, lock.yml and pr-compliance.yml declare one. ci.yml:190 passes secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN to the mutable-ref coverallsapp/github-action@v2 at line 188, and lines 253, 268 and 389 pass it to further third-party actions. image_actions.yml:42 runs peter-evans/create-pull-request@v8 on the inherited token, which requires contents and pull-requests write to function at all.
- .github/workflows/ci.yml:190

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-3 external → ci-cd-pipeline (internet-facing): tb-3 names GITHUB_TOKEN scope as its enforcement point, but ci.yml declares no permissions block, so the token crossing into third-party action code carries the unbounded repository default scope.

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-040 (F-040)
threats.mitigation:
M-038 — Apply least-privilege permissions (priority P2, effort Low)
1. Add a top-level `permissions: {contents: read}` block to .github/workflows/ci.yml and .github/workflows/image_actions.yml, then re-grant only the narrower scopes each job needs at job level — for example contents: write and pull-requests: write on the image_actions build job that runs peter-evans/create-pull-request.
2. Set the repository and organisation default workflow permissions to read-only in GitHub settings so a future workflow that omits the block cannot silently inherit write access.
3. Add a workflow-lint step (zizmor or actionlint) that fails when a workflow file contains no permissions: key.
Verification: Run `grep -L 'permissions:' .github/workflows/*.yml`; expect ci.yml and image_actions.yml to no longer appear in the list of files lacking a permissions declaration.
Reference: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/security-for-github-actions/security-guides/automatic-token-authentication#permissions-for-the-github_token

threats.title: [F-046] Remote install script piped to shell (.github/workflows/ci.yml:358)
threats.description:
The heroku job downloads https://cli-assets.heroku.com/install.sh and pipes it straight into sh with no checksum, signature, or version pin. An attacker who compromises that distribution host, or who can influence DNS or TLS interception for the runner, substitutes the script and executes arbitrary code in a job that goes on to use secrets.HEROKU_API_KEY at line 371, taking over the production and staging deployment credentials.

Impact: Code from an external host executes with the deployment job's privileges and reaches the Heroku API key, giving an attacker control of the juice-shop and juice-shop-staging deployments.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Low, impact High)
CWE: CWE-494
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: stride

Evidence:
.github/workflows/ci.yml:358 runs `curl https://cli-assets.heroku.com/install.sh | sh` with no integrity verification; the same job supplies secrets.HEROKU_API_KEY to the deploy step at line 371 and is reached on every push to develop and master (line 351).
- .github/workflows/ci.yml:358

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-046 (F-046)
threats.mitigation:
M-044 — Verify the Heroku CLI download by checksum before executing it (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Replace the pipe-to-shell at .github/workflows/ci.yml:358 with a download to a file, a `sha256sum --check` against a pinned digest for a pinned CLI version, and only then execute it; or install the CLI from a SHA-pinned action or an npm dependency covered by the lockfile.
2. Add a job step asserting the installed CLI version matches the pinned version so a silent upstream change fails the build rather than shipping.
Verification: Tamper with the pinned checksum value in a branch build; expect the heroku job to fail at the sha256sum step before any step that references secrets.HEROKU_API_KEY runs.
Reference: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/494.html

threats.title: [F-047] Unpinned container base image (Dockerfile:1)
threats.description:
Both build stages resolve their base image by floating reference rather than digest, so the bytes a build consumes are whatever the registry serves at that moment. An attacker who compromises the upstream image or the registry path substitutes a backdoored layer, and the next docker job build bakes it into the published bkimminich/juice-shop image with no build-time signal that the base changed.

Impact: A substituted base image ships inside the container that every deployment of the project runs, giving the attacker code execution in the runtime image without touching the repository.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Low, impact High)
CWE: CWE-1104
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: stride

Evidence:
Dockerfile:1 declares `FROM node:24 AS installer`, a floating tag with no digest, and Dockerfile:22 declares `FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs24-debian13` with neither a tag nor a digest, so it resolves to :latest. This Dockerfile is the file the publish job builds from (.github/workflows/ci.yml:341). docker-compose.test.yml:7 likewise references bkimminich/juice-shop:latest for the docker-test job.
- Dockerfile:1

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-047 (F-047)
threats.mitigation:
M-045 — Pin the container base image to an immutable digest (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Change Dockerfile:1 to `FROM node:24@sha256:<digest> AS installer` and Dockerfile:22 to `FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs24-debian13@sha256:<digest>`, recording the digests resolved at pin time.
2. Add Dependabot or Renovate coverage for the docker ecosystem so digest bumps arrive as reviewable pull requests instead of silent drift.
Verification: Run `grep -n '^FROM' Dockerfile`; expect every line to contain an @sha256: digest.
Reference: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1104.html

threats.title: [F-048] Only mutable image tags published (.github/workflows/ci.yml:345)
threats.description:
The publish step pushes exactly one tag per branch, latest or snapshot, and overwrites it on every subsequent build. After a suspected build compromise nobody can fetch the artifact that was actually deployed, because the tag now points at a newer image and no immutable version tag or digest record was ever published. The attacker's build is indistinguishable from a clean one once the next push completes.

Impact: Post-incident reconstruction of which commit produced a deployed image is impossible from the registry alone, and there is no rollback target, so a supply-chain compromise cannot be scoped or attributed.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-778
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: stride

Evidence:
.github/workflows/ci.yml:331 and 333 set DOCKER_TAG to latest or snapshot and line 345 pushes bkimminich/juice-shop:${{ env.DOCKER_TAG }} as the only tag; no semantic version tag, digest pin, or attestation is recorded, confirmed by a zero-hit search of the file for provenance, attest, id-token and sbom:. The VCS_REF label written at Dockerfile:35 is readable only from an image copy that can still be retrieved.
- .github/workflows/ci.yml:345

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-048 (F-048)
threats.mitigation:
M-046 — Add security audit logging (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Extend the tags: list at .github/workflows/ci.yml:344-345 to also push bkimminich/juice-shop:${{ github.sha }} and the package.json version, so every build leaves a permanently addressable artifact.
2. Record the resulting image digest in the workflow run output or a release note so a deployed image can later be matched to its source commit.
Verification: After a develop build, run `docker buildx imagetools inspect bkimminich/juice-shop:<commit-sha>`; expect the immutable per-commit tag to resolve instead of returning a manifest-unknown error.
Reference: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/778.html

threats.title: [F-057] Org-admin PAT exposed to PR trigger (.github/workflows/pr-compliance.yml:438)
threats.description:
Any GitHub user can open or edit a pull request and thereby start the pr-compliance workflow, which runs on pull_request_target in the privileged base-repository context and places the organization-administration token ORG_ADMIN_TOKEN into a step environment. Because the trigger is reachable by an unauthenticated internet user rather than only by trusted contributors, a single script-injection or action-compromise defect anywhere in this workflow exposes a credential that administers the whole juice-shop organization, not just this repository.

Impact: Compromise of this workflow yields an organization-administration credential rather than a repository-scoped one, letting an attacker administer every juice-shop repository and membership, far beyond the blast radius of the build itself.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Low, impact High)
CWE: CWE-522
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: stride

Evidence:
.github/workflows/pr-compliance.yml:4 triggers on pull_request_target for opened, edited and reopened events, which grants the privileged base-repo context to workflow runs initiated by arbitrary pull-request authors; line 438 injects secrets.ORG_ADMIN_TOKEN into the Block Spammer step, and lines 445-452 show it is a token with org-wide member-blocking authority. Attacker-controlled pull_request title and body values flow through the workflow at lines 289 and 424.
- .github/workflows/pr-compliance.yml:438

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-3 external → ci-cd-pipeline (internet-facing): tb-3 assumes workflow runs start only from verified identities on permitted branches, but pull_request_target lets any pull-request author start this privileged run holding an org-admin credential.

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-057 (F-057)
threats.mitigation:
M-055 — Move ORG_ADMIN_TOKEN out of the pull_request_target workflow in pr-compliance.y… (priority P3, effort Medium)
1. Remove secrets.ORG_ADMIN_TOKEN from .github/workflows/pr-compliance.yml:438 and move the blocking action into a separate workflow_dispatch or repository_dispatch workflow that no externally triggered event can start, or replace the PAT with a GitHub App installation token scoped to the single blocking permission.
2. Add an environment: with required reviewers to whichever job retains the org-admin credential so its use requires an approval gate.
3. Add a workflow-lint assertion (zizmor or actionlint) that fails when a pull_request_target workflow references any secret other than GITHUB_TOKEN.
Verification: Run `grep -n 'secrets\.' .github/workflows/pr-compliance.yml`; expect only secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN and secrets.SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL to remain, with no ORG_ADMIN_TOKEN reference.
Reference: https://securitylab.github.com/resources/github-actions-preventing-pwn-requests/

data.name: Web3 / Wallet / NFT Surface
data.description: Blockchain/web3 endpoints handling wallet addresses, NFT minting, and on-chain key material (ethers). Internet-facing crypto-asset surface with its own key-handling and ownership-verification trust boundary.

threats.title: [F-013] Hard-coded BIP39 wallet mnemonic (routes/checkKeys.ts:10)
threats.description:
An attacker reads `routes/checkKeys.ts:10`, where the twelve-word BIP39 mnemonic for the application's Ethereum wallet is embedded as a string literal, and reproduces the derivation the server performs at line 11 to obtain the wallet's private key. Holding the key, the attacker signs arbitrary transactions as the application's on-chain identity and also satisfies the server's own key check at line 18.

Impact: Full and irrevocable compromise of the Ethereum wallet this component manages: anyone with read access to the source can drain its balance, transfer or mint assets under the application's on-chain identity, and forge proof of key custody. Because the mnemonic is committed to version control, rotation requires migrating to an entirely new wallet.

Risk: Critical (likelihood High, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-798
CVSS v4: 9.3 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N)
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
`routes/checkKeys.ts:10` assigns a complete twelve-word BIP39 mnemonic to a source-level constant, line 11 derives an `HDNodeWallet` from it, and line 12 reads out the private key; the secret is fully recoverable from the source file alone.
- routes/checkKeys.ts:10

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-013 (F-013)
threats.mitigation:
M-013 — Move secrets to a managed secret store (priority P1, effort Medium)
1. Treat the committed wallet as permanently compromised: generate a replacement wallet in a KMS or HSM-backed signer, move any remaining assets, and retire the old address.
2. Delete the mnemonic literal at `routes/checkKeys.ts:10` and load key material at runtime from the platform secret manager; where the route only needs to compare a submitted value, store a salted hash of the expected key and compare against that instead of holding the key in process memory.
3. Purge the mnemonic from git history and add a secret-scanning step to CI that fails the build on BIP39 mnemonic and private-key patterns.
4. Add a test asserting that no twelve-word mnemonic or 0x-prefixed 64-hex-character literal appears under routes/.
Verification: Run the CI secret scan over `routes/` and assert zero findings, and run the new unit test asserting no BIP39 mnemonic or private-key literal is present in `routes/checkKeys.ts`; both must pass on a clean checkout.
Reference: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/798.html

threats.title: [F-043] Unverified wallet ownership claim (routes/nftMint.ts:41)
threats.description:
An anonymous internet attacker reads the public Sepolia `NFTMinted` event log, copies the wallet address of a genuine minter, and POSTs it as `walletAddress` to the `walletNFTVerify` route. The handler at `routes/nftMint.ts:41` takes the address straight from `req.body` and at line 42 tests only whether that string is present in the `addressesMinted` set, so the attacker is credited with an NFT mint performed by a wallet he does not control.

Impact: Wallet-ownership verification — the component's stated security role — is defeated. An attacker uses public on-chain data to claim any NFT-gated status or benefit; the legitimate minter's entry is deleted at line 43, so the real owner can no longer claim it.

Risk: Medium (likelihood High, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-290
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
routes/nftMint.ts:41 assigns req.body.walletAddress directly to metamaskAddress and line 42 uses it as the sole input to the ownership decision; no nonce challenge, signature recovery, or session-to-wallet binding appears anywhere in the handler.
- routes/nftMint.ts:41

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-1 external → api-server (internet-facing): The tb-1 authorization leg assumes each accessed resource is checked against the authenticated user's identity; this handler decides NFT ownership purely from a client-supplied wallet address.

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-043 (F-043)
threats.mitigation:
M-041 — Require a signed wallet nonce (priority P3, effort Medium)
1. Issue a server-generated, single-use nonce per session and require the client to POST the nonce signed by the wallet's private key; in walletNFTVerify recover the signer with ethers verifyMessage and compare the recovered address to req.body.walletAddress before consulting addressesMinted.
2. Bind the verified address to the authenticated session record instead of a process-wide `Set`, and reject the request when the recovered signer differs from the claimed address or the nonce has already been consumed.
3. Add an integration test that POSTs a known minter address without a valid signature and asserts a 401 response and no state change to `addressesMinted`.
Verification: Run the new integration test: `POST /rest/web3/nftMint` style verify request carrying a third party's minter address and no signature must return 401 and leave `addressesMinted` unchanged; a request carrying a correctly signed nonce for that address must return 200.
Reference: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/290.html

threats.title: [F-044] Open redirect to unallowlisted host (routes/redirect.ts:19)
threats.description:
An attacker crafts a /redirect?to=<attacker URL> link that satisfies security.isRedirectAllowed() without matching any allowlist prefix, and the handler sends the victim to the attacker's site via res.redirect(toUrl) at routes/redirect.ts:19. Because the link originates on the Juice Shop origin, it lends the phishing page the application's reputation and is usable to harvest wallet or account credentials in the Web3 flows this component serves.

Impact: Users following a link on the application's own origin land on an attacker-controlled page, enabling credential and wallet-seed phishing and exfiltration of tokens carried in the redirect chain.

Risk: Medium (likelihood High, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-601
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
routes/redirect.ts:19 redirects to the raw query parameter, and line 18 solves redirectChallenge precisely when isUnintendedRedirect(toUrl) is true — a condition that requires toUrl to start with none of security.redirectAllowlist (lines 27-32) while having already passed isRedirectAllowed at line 16. The file therefore proves the allowlist check is weaker than prefix matching.
- routes/redirect.ts:19

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-044 (F-044)
threats.mitigation:
M-042 — Validate redirect targets against an allowlist (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Parse toUrl with the WHATWG URL API and redirect only when the parsed origin exactly equals an entry in security.redirectAllowlist; reject any value that fails to parse, uses a scheme other than https, or carries userinfo.
2. Replace the substring-style check behind isRedirectAllowed with the exact-origin comparison so lines 16 and 27-32 can no longer disagree about what is allowed.
3. Add a test matrix covering https://evil.test/?to=https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop, //evil.test, and https://github.com.evil.test asserting HTTP 406 for each.
Verification: GET /redirect?to=https://evil.test/%3Fto%3Dhttps://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop must return 406 with no Location header; GET /redirect?to=https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop must still return 302 to that exact URL.
Reference: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/601.html

threats.title: [F-066] Credit granted on unowned wallet key (routes/web3Wallet.ts:27)
threats.description:
An attacker registers wallet addresses he does not control through the contractExploitListener route, then waits for any of those addresses to trigger the on-chain ContractExploited event. The listener at routes/web3Wallet.ts:27 gates the privilege solely on membership in walletsConnected, a set populated from unauthenticated request bodies, so the attacker is granted the exploit credit earned by a third party's wallet.

Impact: The wallet address acts as a user-controlled authorization key, so an attacker obtains on-chain-exploit credit without controlling the wallet that performed the action, and line 28 removes the entry so the wallet's real owner cannot be credited.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-639
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
routes/web3Wallet.ts:27 tests walletsConnected.has(exploiter) as the only authorization condition and line 29 then solves the challenge unconditionally; the set is filled at line 16 straight from req.body.walletAddress with no signature check and no binding to the requesting session.
- routes/web3Wallet.ts:27

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-1 external → api-server (internet-facing): The tb-1 authorization leg assumes each accessed resource is checked against the authenticated user's identity; this decision uses only a wallet address supplied earlier by an unauthenticated request body.

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-066 (F-066)
threats.mitigation:
M-064 — Enforce object-level (ownership) authorization (priority P3, effort Medium)
1. Accept a registration only when the request carries a server-issued single-use nonce signed by the wallet, recover the signer with ethers verifyMessage, and store the registration under the authenticated session rather than a global Set.
2. In the ContractExploited handler, resolve the exploiter address to the session that proved control of it and grant the credit to that session only, failing closed when no verified binding exists.
3. Add an integration test that registers a third party's address without a signature, emits a simulated ContractExploited event for it, and asserts no credit is granted.
Verification: Run the new integration test: an unsigned registration followed by a simulated ContractExploited event for that address must leave the challenge unsolved, while a signed registration for the same address must solve it.
Reference: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/639.html
